query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In non-equilibrium, Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys, thermal activation or service exposure induces Mg segregation that promotes the formation of a dual-phase microstructure—a primarily solid solution matrix with discrete, Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates. These precipitates act as localized barriers that modify the kinetics of oxide scale formation and enhance the corrosion passivation behavior, thereby improving high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the as-cast, homogeneous structure.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast or induction-melted Mg-containing high-entropy alloy with a predominantly solid solution microstructure and minimal intermetallic phase formation, maintaining a density below 6 g/cm³.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled thermal aging or high-temperature exposure that simulates long-term service conditions.
generation.conditions: Corrosion tests conducted in a standardized electrolyte at room temperature and high-temperature oxidation tests at temperatures (e.g., 600–800 °C) in an oxidizing atmosphere, under conditions that do not trigger complete phase separation or excessive grain coarsening.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of discrete Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates along grain boundaries and interdendritic regions resulting from Mg segregation during thermal exposure.
generation.mechanism: Mg atoms, initially homogeneously distributed, diffuse under thermal activation to form metastable Mg-rich intermetallic phases. These phases modify local chemical gradients and increase the density of phase boundaries, which act as preferential sites for the nucleation and adhesion of protective oxide films, thereby altering both the corrosion behavior at ambient conditions and the oxidation kinetics at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast baseline, the thermally aged alloy will exhibit a refined microstructure with well-distributed Mg-rich precipitates, resulting in reduced corrosion current densities and improved formation of adherent, protective oxides during high-temperature oxidation tests.
generation.baseline: The initial, non-aged state of the alloy with a homogeneous solid solution and minimal intermetallic phase presence.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies when the applied thermal treatment is sufficient to initiate metastable phase separation (without complete coarsening or degradation of mechanical integrity) and within the density constraint (<6 g/cm³).
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of Mg segregation and the morphology, distribution, and chemical composition of the resulting intermetallic precipitates are not fully determined; additionally, potential interactions with other alloying elements may modify the proposed mechanism and its impact on corrosion and oxidation behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy samples with densities below 6 g/cm³: one in the as-cast non-equilibrium state and the other subjected to controlled thermal aging (e.g., held at 700 °C for various durations such as 10, 30, and 60 hours). Characterize each sample set via microstructural analysis (using SEM, TEM, and XRD) to detect the formation of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates. Subsequently, conduct standardized potentiodynamic corrosion tests and high-temperature oxidation tests (in air) to evaluate changes in corrosion current density and oxide layer properties.
measurements: Microstructural phase identification and precipitate distribution (via SEM/TEM/XRD)
Corrosion current density and potential (via potentiodynamic polarization)
Oxide scale thickness, adhesion, and composition (via high-temperature oxidation tests and surface analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally aged samples do not reveal a significant formation of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates compared to the as-cast state, or if no measurable improvement (or a degradation) in corrosion performance and high-temperature oxidation resistance is observed relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Evaluation of Equiatomic CrMnFeCoNiCu System and Subsequent Derivation of a Non-Equiatomic MnFeCoNiCu Alloy

Abstract: AbstractInvestigation into non-equiatomic high-entropy alloys has grown in recent years due to questions about the role of entropy stabilization in forming single-phase solid solutions. Non-equiatomic alloys have been shown to retain the outstanding mechanical properties exhibited by their equiatomic counterparts and even improve electrical, thermal, and magnetic properties, albeit with relaxed composition bounds. However, much remains to understand the processing–structure–property relationships in all classes of so-called high-entropy alloys (HEAs). Here, we are motivated by the natural phenomena of crystal growth and equilibrium conditions to introduce a method of HEA development where controlled processing conditions determine the most probable and stable composition. This is demonstrated by cooling an equiatomic CrMnFeCoNiCu alloy from the melt steadily over 3 days (cooling rate ~4 °C/h). Effect of Al Content and Local Chemical Order on the Stacking Fault Energy in Ti–V–Zr–Nb–Al High-Entropy Alloys Based on First Principles

Abstract: AbstractAs a promising candidate for next-generation aviation structural materials, lightweight refractory high entropy alloys (HEAs) exhibit high strength, low density, and excellent high-temperature performance. In this study, we investigated the influence of local chemical ordering on the properties of Ti–V–Zr–Nb–Al HEAs using Monte Carlo (MC) simulations based on density functional theory (DFT) calculations. We established that the chemical short-range ordering (SRO) in Ti–V–Zr–Nb–Al HEAs increases with the Al content, resulting in a gradual increase in stacking fault energy (SFE). Designing TiZrNbTa-Al Medium-Entropy Alloy for Next-Generation Hydrogen Storage

Abstract: Medium-entropy alloys (MEAs) represent a promising class of materials for solid-state hydrogen storage due to their high hydrogen affinity, structural stability, and tunable properties. In this work, a compositional series of (TiZrNbTa){100−x}Alx (x = 0–10 at. %) MEAs were prepared and systematically investigated to clarify the influence of aluminum addition on microstructure, mechanical response, and hydrogen sorption behavior. The alloys were synthesized by arc melting, homogenized by annealing, and characterized using microscopy, X-ray diffraction, density measurements, microhardness testing, nanoindentation, and hydrogen absorption/desorption experiments. Hydrogen sorption was evaluated by isobaric absorption measurements at 2 MPa H2 over two consecutive cycles, complemented by thermogravimetric desorption analysis of hydrogenated samples. The results show that aluminum addition significantly affects activation behavior, hydrogen uptake, and residual hydrogen retention, while simultaneously increasing hardness and elastic modulus in a non-linear manner. On the evolving nature of c/a ratio in a hexagonal close-packed epsilon martensite phase in transformative high entropy alloys

Abstract: Activation of different slip systems in hexagonal close packed (h.c.p.) metals depends primarily on the c/a ratio, which is an intrinsic property that can be altered through alloying addition. In conventional h.c.p. alloys where there is no diffusion-less phase transformation and associated transformation volume change with deformation, the c/a ratio remains constant during deformation. In the present study, c/a ratio and transformation volume change of h.c.p. epsilon martensite phase in transformative high entropy alloys (HEAs) were quantified as functions of alloy chemistry, friction stir processing and tensile deformation. The study revealed that while intrinsic c/a is dependent on alloying elements, c/a of epsilon in transformative HEAs changes with processing and deformation. This is attributed to transformation volume change induced dependence of h.c.p. lattice parameters on microstructure and stress state. Lower than ideal c/a ratio promotes non-basal pyramidal 〈c + a〉 slip and deformation twinning in epsilon phase of transformative HEAs.

The Effect of Scandium Ternary Intergrain Precipitates in Al-Containing High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: We investigate the effect of alloying with scandium on microstructure, high-temperature phase stability, electron transport, and mechanical properties of the Al2CoCrFeNi, Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi, and AlCoCrCu0.5FeNi high-entropy alloys. Out of the three model alloys, Al2CoCrFeNi adopts a disordered CsCl structure type. Both of the six-component alloys contain a mixture of body-centered cubic (bcc) and face centered cubic (fcc) phases. The comparison between in situ high-temperature powder diffraction data and ex situ data from heat-treated samples highlights the presence of a reversible bcc to fcc transition. The precipitation of a MgZn2-type intermetallic phase along grain boundaries following scandium addition affects all systems differently, but especially enhances the properties of Al2CoCrFeNi. It causes grain refinement; hardness and electrical conductivity increases (up to 20% and 14% respectively) and affects the CsCl-type → fcc equilibrium by moving the transformation to sensibly higher temperatures. The maximum dimensionless thermoelectric figure of merit (ZT) of 0.014 is reached
